facts.title: Born From Radium's Breath
facts.text: Radon was discovered in 1899-1900 by Ernest Rutherford and Robert B. Owens, who noticed a radioactive 'emanation' coming off thorium, while Friedrich Ernst Dorn independently observed the same gas escaping from radium. Because it seeped out of radium it was first called 'radium emanation' or 'niton,' and only in 1923 did it receive the official name radon. Its name literally points to its parent: it is the gaseous offspring of decaying radium.

facts.title: The Heaviest Gas You'll Meet
facts.text: Radon is the densest noble gas and one of the densest gases known, roughly 7.5 times heavier than air, which is why it tends to pool in basements, mines, and low-lying enclosed spaces. A single liter weighs about 9.7 grams at standard conditions. This heaviness, combined with being colorless and odorless, makes it impossible to detect by human senses alone.

facts.title: A Noble Gas That Reacts
facts.text: Although noble gases are famous for being chemically aloof, radon is reactive enough to form compounds, most notably radon difluoride (RnF2), which forms readily when radon meets fluorine. This happens because radon's outer electrons are so far from the nucleus that they are loosely held and easier to coax into bonding. Studying these fragile compounds is extremely hard, since the radon decays away even as chemists try to work with it.

facts.title: It Literally Glows
facts.text: In high enough concentrations radon and the air around it can emit a faint luminescence, and when chilled the gas glows yellow, deepening to an orange-red as it approaches its very low temperatures. This glow comes from the intense radiation it emits exciting the surrounding atoms. Early researchers described frozen radon shining like a tiny radioactive lantern.

facts.title: The Four-Day Half-Life
facts.text: The most common isotope, radon-222, has a half-life of just 3.82 days, meaning half of any sample vanishes through radioactive decay in under four days. This makes radon a fleeting element: it is constantly being created by decaying radium and constantly disappearing. Because it is so short-lived, there is no stable form of radon anywhere in nature.

facts.title: Seeping Up From Granite
facts.text: Radon forms naturally underground as uranium and radium in rocks and soil decay, and it is especially abundant where there is granite, shale, or phosphate-rich bedrock. The gas escapes through cracks and pores and can accumulate inside buildings, particularly in poorly ventilated basements. This is why some regions, such as parts of the Appalachian mountains and Cornwall in England, have notably high indoor radon levels.

facts.title: A Leading Cause of Lung Cancer
facts.text: Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking, and the leading cause among people who have never smoked, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the World Health Organization. The danger comes not from radon itself but from its solid radioactive decay products, which lodge in the lungs and bombard tissue with radiation. Millions of homes are tested and ventilated each year specifically to keep radon exposure low.

facts.title: Once Used to Fight Cancer
facts.text: Before modern radiotherapy, hospitals sealed radon gas into tiny gold capsules called 'radon seeds' and implanted them in tumors to kill cancer cells with radiation. This was a direct extension of radium therapy, using the more convenient gas form. The practice has largely been abandoned in favor of safer, more controllable radiation sources, but it represents a striking early chapter in nuclear medicine.

facts.title: An Earthquake Early Warning
facts.text: Scientists monitor radon levels in soil gas, groundwater, and wells because surges in radon are sometimes detected before earthquakes, as shifting rock opens new pathways for the gas to escape. Researchers in countries including Japan and Italy have studied these anomalies as a possible piece of an earthquake prediction puzzle. While not yet a reliable standalone forecast, radon remains a fascinating natural tracer of what is happening deep underground.

facts.title: A Tracer For Air And Water
facts.text: Because radon is chemically inert and decays at a precisely known rate, scientists use it as a natural tracer to study how air moves through soil, how water flows underground, and how gases mix in the atmosphere. By measuring radon, geologists can map fault lines and hydrologists can track where groundwater connects to rivers and oceans. Its steady radioactive clock turns an invisible gas into a powerful scientific measuring tool.
